{{Short description|Non-linear partial differential equation encountered in problems of wave propagation}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2023}}
An '''eikonal equation''' (from [[Ancient Greek|Greek]] εἰκών, image<ref>The Oxford English Dictionary. 2nd ed. 1989. OED Online. Oxford University Press. 4 April 2000 http://dictionary.oed.com/cgi/entry/00292404</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Evans |first=L. C. |title=Partial Differential Equations |series=AMS Graduate Texts in Mathematics |volume=19 |page=93 }}</ref>) is a [[Nonlinear partial differential equation|non-linear]] [[first-order partial differential equation]] that is encountered in problems of [[wave propagation]].

The classical eikonal equation in [[geometric optics]] is a differential equation of the form

{{NumBlk|:|<math>|\nabla u(x)|=n(x)</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

where <math>x</math> lies in an open subset of <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>, <math>n(x)</math> is a 
positive function,  <math>\nabla</math>  denotes the [[gradient]], and <math>| \cdot |</math> is the [[Euclidean norm#Euclidean norm|Euclidean norm]]. The function <math> n </math> is given and one seeks solutions <math> u </math>.
In the context of [[geometric optics]], the function <math> n </math> is the [[refractive index]] of the medium.

More generally, an eikonal equation is an equation of the form

{{NumBlk|:|<math>H(x,\nabla u(x)) = 0 </math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}

where <math> H </math> is a function of <math> 2n </math> variables. 
Here the function <math> H </math> is given, and  <math> u </math> is the solution.
If <math> H(x,y)=  |y| - n(x) </math>, then equation ({{EquationNote|2}}) becomes ({{EquationNote|1}}).

Eikonal equations naturally arise in the [[WKB method]]<ref>{{cite book
|last1=Dimassi |first1=Mouez  |last2=Sjöstrand  |first2=Johannes |title=Spectral asymptotics in the semi-classical limit |series=London Math. Society Lecture Notes 268. |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1999 |isbn=0-521-66544-2}}</ref>
and the study of [[Maxwell's equations]].<ref>{{citation  |last=Rauch |first=Jeffrey |title=Hyperbolic partial differential equations and geometric optics |series=Graduate Studies in Mathematics, 133 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |year=2012 |bibcode=2012hpde.book.....R |isbn=978-0-8218-7291-8}}</ref> Eikonal equations provide a link between [[physical optics|physical (wave) optics]] and [[geometric optics|geometric (ray) optics]].

One fast computational algorithm to approximate the solution to the eikonal equation is the [[fast marching method]].

==History==

The term "eikonal" was first used in the context of geometric optics by [[Heinrich Bruns]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Bruns |first=Heinrich |title=Das Eikonal |publisher=S. Hirzel |year=1895}}</ref> However, 
the actual equation appears earlier in the seminal work of [[William Rowan Hamilton]] on [[geometric optics]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Hamilton |first=William Rowan  |date=1828 |title=Theory of Systems of Rays |url=https://www.emis.de/classics/Hamilton/index.html |journal=Transactions of the Royal Irish Academy |volume=15 |pages=69–174}}</ref>

==Physical interpretation==

===Continuous shortest-path problems===

Suppose that <math> \Omega </math> is an open set with suitably smooth boundary <math> \partial \Omega</math>. 
The solution to the eikonal equation

:<math>\left|\nabla u(x)\right| = \frac 1 {f(x)} \text{ for } x \in \Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n,</math>
:<math>u(x) = q(x) \text{ for } x \in \partial\Omega</math>

can be interpreted as the minimal amount of time required to travel from <math>x</math> to <math>\partial \Omega</math>, where <math>f: \bar{\Omega} \to (0, +\infty)</math> is the speed of travel, and <math>q: \partial\Omega \to [0, +\infty)</math> is an exit-time penalty. (Alternatively this can be posed as a minimal cost-to-exit by making the right-side <math>C(x)/f(x)</math> and <math>q</math> an exit-cost penalty.)

In the special case when <math>f=1</math> and <math>q=0</math>, the solution gives the [[signed distance]] from  <math>\partial \Omega</math>.<ref>Sakai, Takashi. "On Riemannian manifolds admitting a function whose gradient is of constant norm." Kodai Mathematical Journal 19.1 (1996): 39-51.
</ref>

By assuming that <math>\nabla u(x)</math> exists at all points, it is easy to prove that <math>u(x)</math> corresponds to a time-optimal control problem using [[Bellman equation#Bellman.27s principle of optimality|Bellman's optimality principle]] and a Taylor expansion.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Z. |last1=Clawson |first2=A. |last2=Chacon |first3=A. |last3=Vladimirsky |title=Causal Domain Restriction for Eikonal Equations |journal=SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing |volume=36 |issue=5 |pages=A2478–A2505 |year=2014 |arxiv=1309.2884 |doi=10.1137/130936531 |bibcode=2014SJSC...36A2478C |s2cid=17226196 }}</ref> Unfortunately, it is not guaranteed that <math>\nabla u(x)</math> exists at all points, and more advanced techniques are necessary to prove this. This led to the development of [[viscosity solution]]s in the 1980s by [[Pierre-Louis Lions]] and [[Michael G. Crandall]],<ref>{{cite book |first1=M. |last1=Bardi |first2=I. |last2=Capuzzo-Dolcetta |title=Optimal Control and Viscosity Solutions of Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman Equations |location=Boston |publisher=Birkhäuser |year=1997 |isbn=0-8176-3640-4 }}</ref> and Lions won a [[Fields Medal]] for his contributions.

===Electromagnetic potential===
The physical meaning of the eikonal equation is related to the formula

: <math> \mathbf E = -\nabla V, </math>

where <math>\mathbf E</math> is the [[electric field]] strength, and <math>V</math> is the [[electric potential]].  There is a similar equation for velocity potential in fluid flow and temperature in heat transfer.  The physical meaning of this equation in the electromagnetic example is that any charge in the region is pushed to move at right angles to the lines{{clarify|reason=Why are these lines?|date=May 2015}} of constant potential, and along lines of force determined by the field of the '''E''' vector and the sign of the charge.

Ray optics and electromagnetism are related by the fact that the eikonal equation gives a second electromagnetic formula of the same form as the potential equation above where the line of constant potential has been replaced by a line of constant phase, and the force lines have been replaced by normal vectors coming out of the constant phase line at right angles.  The magnitude of these normal vectors is given by the square root of the relative permittivity.  The line of constant phase can be considered the edge of one of the advancing light waves (''[[wavefront]]'').  The normal vectors are the rays the light is traveling down in ray optics.

==Computational algorithms==

Several fast and efficient algorithms to solve the eikonal equation have been developed since the 1990s. Many of these algorithms take advantage of algorithms developed much earlier for [[shortest path problem]]s on graphs with nonnegative edge lengths.<ref name="chacon_twoscale">{{cite journal |first1=A. |last1=Chacon |first2=A. |last2=Vladimirsky |title=Fast two-scale methods for eikonal equations |journal=SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing |volume=34 |issue=2 |pages=A547–A578 |year=2012 |doi=10.1137/10080909X |arxiv=1110.6220 |bibcode=2012SJSC...34A.547C |s2cid=6404391 }}</ref> These algorithms take advantage of the [[Causality#Science|causality]] provided by the physical interpretation and typically discretize the domain using a [[Finite element method#Discretization|mesh]]<ref name="kimmel_sethian1">{{cite journal |first1=R. |last1=Kimmel |first2=J. A. |last2=Sethian |title=Computing Geodesic Paths on Manifolds |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=95 |issue=15 |pages=8431–8435 |year=1998 |doi=10.1073/pnas.95.15.8431 |pmid=9671694 |pmc=21092 |bibcode=1998PNAS...95.8431K |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="bronsteins_kimmel1">{{cite journal |first1=A. M. |last1=Bronstein |first2=M. M. |last2=Bronstein |first3=R. |last3=Kimmel |title=Weighted distance maps computation on parametric three-dimensional manifolds |journal=Journal of Computational Physics |volume=225 |issue=1 |pages=771–784 |year=2007 |doi=10.1016/j.jcp.2007.01.009 |bibcode=2007JCoPh.225..771B }}</ref><ref name="sethian_vlad_fmm_mesh">{{cite journal |first1=J. A. |last1=Sethian |first2=A. |last2=Vladimirsky |title=Fast methods for the Eikonal and related Hamilton–Jacobi equations on unstructured meshes |journal=Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA |volume=97 |issue=11 |pages=5699–5703 |year=2000 |doi=10.1073/pnas.090060097 |pmid=10811874 |pmc=18495 |bibcode=2000PNAS...97.5699S |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="yershov_fmm_mesh">{{cite journal |first1=D. S. |last1=Yershov |first2=S. M. |last2=LaValle |title=Simplicial Dijkstra and A* Algorithms: From Graphs to Continuous Spaces |journal=Advanced Robotics |volume=26 |issue=17 |pages=2065–2085 |year=2012 |doi=10.1080/01691864.2012.729559 |s2cid=17573584 }}</ref> or [[regular grid]]<ref name="sethian_fmm">{{cite journal |first=J. A. |last=Sethian |title=A Fast Marching Level Set Method for Monotonically Advancing Fronts |journal=Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. |volume=93 |issue=4 |pages=1591–1595 |year=1996 |doi=10.1073/pnas.93.4.1591 |pmid=11607632 |pmc=39986 |bibcode=1996PNAS...93.1591S |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="tsitsiklis_fmm">{{cite journal |first=J. N. |last=Tsitsiklis |title=Efficient algorithms for globally optimal trajectories |journal=IEEE Trans. Autom. Control |volume=40 |issue=9 |pages=1528–1538 |year=1995 |doi=10.1109/9.412624 |hdl=1721.1/3340 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> and calculate the solution at each discretized point.
Eikonal solvers on triangulated surfaces were introduced by Kimmel and Sethian in 1998.<ref name="kimmel_sethian1" /><ref name="bronsteins_kimmel1" />

Sethian's '''[[fast marching method]] (FMM)'''<ref name="sethian_fmm" /><ref name="tsitsiklis_fmm" /> was the first "fast and efficient" algorithm created to solve the Eikonal equation. The original description discretizes the domain <math>\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n</math> into a regular grid and "marches" the solution from "known" values to the undiscovered regions, precisely mirroring the logic of [[Dijkstra's algorithm]]. If <math>\Omega</math> is discretized and has <math>M</math> meshpoints, then the computational complexity is <math>O(M\log M)</math> where the <math>\log</math> term comes from the use of a heap (typically binary). A number of modifications can be prescribed to FMM since it is classified as a label-setting method. In addition, FMM has been generalized to operate on general meshes that discretize the domain.<ref name="kimmel_sethian1" /><ref name="bronsteins_kimmel1" /><ref name="sethian_vlad_fmm_mesh" /><ref name="yershov_fmm_mesh" />

'''Label-correcting methods''' such as the [[Bellman–Ford algorithm]] can also be used to solve the discretized Eikonal equation also with numerous modifications allowed (e.g. "Small Labels First" <ref name="chacon_twoscale" /><ref name="SLF">{{cite journal |first=D. P. |last=Bertsekas |title=A Simple and Fast Label Correcting Algorithm for Shortest Paths |journal=Networks |volume=23 |issue=8 |pages=703–709 |year=1993 |doi=10.1002/net.3230230808 |hdl=1721.1/3256 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> or "Large Labels Last" <ref name="chacon_twoscale" /><ref name="LLL">{{cite journal |first1=D. P. |last1=Bertsekas |first2=F. |last2=Guerriero |first3=R. |last3=Musmanno |title=Parallel Asynchronous Label Correcting Methods for Shortest Paths |journal=Journal of Optimization Theory and Applications |volume=88 |pages=297–320 |year=1996 |issue=2 |doi=10.1007/BF02192173 |s2cid=13172492 |hdl=1721.1/3390 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>). Two-queue methods have also been developed<ref name="two_queue_and_locking">{{cite journal |first1=S. |last1=Bak |first2=J. |last2=McLaughlin |first3=D. |last3=Renzi |title=Some improvements for the fast sweeping method |journal=SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing  |volume=32 |issue=5 |year=2010 |pages=2853–2874 |doi=10.1137/090749645 |bibcode=2010SJSC...32.2853B }}</ref> that are essentially a version of the Bellman-Ford algorithm except two queues are used with a threshold used to determine which queue a gridpoint should be assigned to based on local information.

Sweeping algorithms such as the '''[[fast sweeping method]] (FSM)'''<ref name="zhao_fsm">{{cite journal |first=H. |last=Zhao |title=A fast sweeping method for eikonal equations |journal=Math. Comp. |volume=74 |year=2004 |issue=250 |pages=603–627 |doi=10.1090/S0025-5718-04-01678-3 |doi-access=free }}</ref> are highly efficient for solving Eikonal equations when the corresponding [[Method of characteristics|characteristic curves]] do not change direction very often.<ref name="chacon_twoscale" /> These algorithms are label-correcting but do not make use of a queue or heap, and instead prescribe different orderings for the gridpoints to be updated and iterate through these orderings until convergence. Some improvements were introduced such as "locking" gridpoints<ref name="two_queue_and_locking" /> during a sweep if does not receive an update, but on highly refined grids and higher-dimensional spaces there is still a large overhead due to having to pass through every gridpoint. Parallel methods have been introduced that attempt to decompose the domain and perform sweeping on each decomposed subset. Zhao's parallel implementation decomposes the domain into <math>n</math>-dimensional subsets and then runs an individual FSM on each subset.<ref name="zhao_fsm_parallel">{{cite journal |first=H. |last=Zhao |title=Parallel Implementations of the Fast Sweeping Method |journal=J. Comput. Math. |volume=25 |issue=4 |pages=421–429 |year=2007 |jstor=43693378 }}</ref> Detrixhe's parallel implementation also decomposes the domain, but parallelizes each individual sweep so that processors are responsible for updating gridpoints in an <math>(n-1)</math>-dimensional [[hyperplane]] until the entire domain is fully swept.<ref name="dextrixhe_fsm_parallel">{{cite journal |first1=M. |last1=Detrixhe |first2=F. |last2=Gibou |first3=C. |last3=Min |title=A parallel fast sweeping method for the Eikonal equation |journal=Journal of Computational Physics |volume=237 |pages=46–55 |year=2013 |doi=10.1016/j.jcp.2012.11.042 |bibcode=2013JCoPh.237...46D }}</ref>

'''Hybrid methods''' have also been introduced that take advantage of FMM's efficiency with FSM's simplicity. For example, the Heap Cell Method (HCM) decomposes the domain into cells and performs FMM on the cell-domain, and each time a "cell" is updated FSM is performed on the local gridpoint-domain that lies within that cell.<ref name="chacon_twoscale" /> A parallelized version of HCM has also been developed.<ref name="chacon_phcm">{{cite journal |first1=A. |last1=Chacon |first2=A. |last2=Vladimirsky |title=A parallel two-scale method for Eikonal equations |journal=SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing |volume=37 |issue=1 |pages=A156–A180 |year=2015 |doi=10.1137/12088197X |arxiv=1306.4743 |bibcode=2015SJSC...37A.156C }}</ref>

==Numerical approximation==

For simplicity assume that <math>\Omega</math> is discretized into a uniform grid with spacings <math>h_x</math> and <math>h_y</math> in the x and y directions, respectively.

===2D approximation on a Cartesian grid===

Assume that a gridpoint <math>x_{ij}</math> has value <math>U_{ij} = U(x_{ij}) \approx u(x_{ij})</math>. A first-order scheme to approximate the partial derivatives is
:<math>\max\left(D_{ij}^{-x}U, -D_{ij}^{+x}U, 0\right)^2 + \max\left(D_{ij}^{-y}U, -D_{ij}^{+y}U, 0\right)^2 \ = \ \frac{1}{f_{ij}^2}</math>
where

:<math>u_x(x_{ij}) \approx D_{ij}^{\pm x} U = \frac{U_{i\pm1,j}-U_{ij}}{\pm h_x} \quad\text{ and }\quad u_y(x_{ij}) \approx D_{ij}^{\pm y} U = \frac{U_{i,j\pm1}-U_{ij}}{\pm h_y}.</math>

Due to the consistent, monotone, and causal properties of this discretization<ref name="chacon_twoscale" /> it is easy to show that if <math>U_X = \min(U_{i-1,j},U_{i+1,j})</math> and <math>U_Y = \min(U_{i,j-1}, U_{i,j+1})</math> and <math>|U_X/h_x-U_Y/h_y| \leq 1/f_{ij}</math> then

:<math>\left(\frac{U_{ij}-U_X}{h_x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{U_{ij}-U_Y}{h_y}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{f_{ij}^2}</math>

which can be solved as a quadratic. In the limiting case of <math>h_x = h_y = h</math>, this reduces to

:<math>U_{ij} = \frac{U_X + U_Y}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{(U_X+U_Y)^2 - 2 \left(U_X^2 + U_Y^2 - \frac{h^2}{f_{ij}^2} \right)}.</math>

This solution will always exist as long as <math>|U_X-U_Y| \leq \sqrt{2}h/f_{ij}</math> is satisfied and is larger than both, <math>U_X</math> and <math>U_Y</math>,  as long as <math>|U_X-U_Y| \leq h/f_{ij}</math> . 

If <math>|U_X/h_x-U_Y/h_y| \geq 1/f_{ij}</math>, a lower-dimensional update must be performed by assuming one of the partial derivatives is <math>0</math>:

:<math>U_{ij} = \min\left(U_X + \frac{h_x}{f_{ij}}, U_Y + \frac{h_y}{f_{ij}}\right).</math>

===''n''-D approximation on a Cartesian grid===

Assume that a grid point <math>x</math> has value <math>U = U(x) \approx u(x)</math>. Repeating the same steps as in the <math>n=2</math> case we can use a first-order scheme to approximate the partial derivatives. Let <math>U_i</math> be the minimum of the values of the neighbors in the <math>\pm\mathbf{e}_i</math> directions, where <math>\mathbf{e}_i</math> is a [[Standard basis|standard unit basis vector]]. The approximation is then

:<math>\sum_{j=1}^n \left(\frac{U-U_j}{h}\right)^2 \ = \ \frac{1}{f_i^2}. </math>

Solving this [[quadratic equation]] for <math>U</math> yields:

:<math>U = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n U_j + \frac{1}{n}\sqrt{\left(\sum_{j=1}^n U_j\right)^2 - n \left(\sum_{j=1}^n U_j^2 - \frac{h^2}{f_i^2}\right)}. </math>

If the discriminant in the square root is negative, then a lower-dimensional update must be performed (i.e. one of the partial derivatives is <math>0</math>).

If <math>n=2</math> then perform the one-dimensional update

:<math>U = \frac{h}{f_i} + \min_{j=1,\ldots,n} U_j. </math>

If <math>n \geq 3</math> then perform an <math>n-1</math> dimensional update using the values <math>\{U_1, \ldots, U_n\} \setminus \{U_i\}</math> for every <math>i=1,\ldots,n</math> and choose the smallest.

==Mathematical description==
{{multiple issues|
{{research paper|section|date=June 2016}}
{{technical|section|date=June 2016}}
{{more footnotes|section|date=June 2016}}
{{original research|section|date=June 2016}}
|section=yes}}
An eikonal equation is one of the form
:<math>H(x,\nabla u(x)) = 0</math>
:<math>u(0,x') = u_0(x'),\text{ for } x = (x_1,x')</math>
The plane <math>x = (0,x')</math> can be thought of as the [[initial condition]], by thinking of <math>x_1</math> as <math>t.</math>  We could also solve the equation on a subset of this plane, or on a curved surface, with obvious modifications.

The eikonal equation shows up in [[geometrical optics]], which is a way of studying solutions of the [[wave equation]] <math>c^2 |\nabla_x u|^2 = |\partial_t u|^2</math>, where <math>c(x)</math> and <math>u(x,t)</math>.  In geometric optics, the eikonal equation describes the phase fronts of waves.  Under reasonable hypothesis on the "initial" data, the eikonal equation admits a local solution, but a global smooth solution (e.g. a solution for all time in the geometrical optics case) is not possible.  The reason is that [[caustic (mathematics)|caustics]] may develop.  In the geometrical optics case, this means that wavefronts cross.

We can solve the eikonal equation using the method of characteristics.  One must impose the "non-characteristic" hypothesis <math>\partial_{p_1} H(x,p) \neq 0</math> along the initial hypersurface <math>x = (0,x')</math>, where ''H''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''H''(''x'',''p'') and ''p''&nbsp;=&nbsp;(''p''<sub>1</sub>,...,''p''<sub>''n''</sub>) is the variable that gets replaced by ∇''u''. Here ''x''&nbsp;=&nbsp;(''x''<sub>1</sub>,...,''x''<sub>''n''</sub>)&nbsp;=&nbsp;(''t'',''x''&prime;).

First, solve the problem <math>H(x,\xi(x)) = 0</math>, <math>\xi(x) = \nabla u(x), x\in H</math>.  This is done by defining curves (and values of <math>\xi</math> on those curves) as
:<math>\dot x(s) = \nabla_\xi H(x(s),\xi(s)), \;\;\;\; \dot \xi(s) = -\nabla_x H(x(s),\xi(s)).</math>
:<math>x(0) = x_0, \;\;\;\; \xi(x(0)) = \nabla u(x(0)).</math>  Note that even before we have a solution <math>u</math>, we know <math>\nabla u(x)</math> for <math>x = (0,x')</math> due to our equation for <math>H</math>.
That these equations have a solution for some interval <math>0 \leq s < s_1</math> follows from standard ODE theorems (using the non-characteristic hypothesis).  These curves fill out an [[open set]] around the plane <math>x = (0,x')</math>.  Thus the curves define the value of <math>\xi</math> in an open set about our initial plane.  Once defined as such it is easy to see using the chain rule that <math>\partial_s H(x(s), \xi(s)) = 0</math>, and therefore <math>H = 0</math> along these curves.

We want our solution <math>u</math> to satisfy <math>\nabla u = \xi</math>, or more specifically, for every <math>s</math>, <math>(\nabla u)(x(s)) = \xi(x(s)).</math>  Assuming for a minute that this is possible, for any solution <math>u(x)</math> we must have

:<math>\frac{d}{d s} u(x(s)) = \nabla u(x(s)) \cdot \dot x(s) = \xi \cdot \frac{\partial H}{\partial \xi}, </math>

and therefore

:<math>u(x(t)) = u(x(0)) + \int_0^t \xi(x(s))\cdot \dot x(s)\, ds.</math>

In other words, the solution <math>u</math> will be given in a neighborhood of the initial plane by an explicit equation.  However, since the different paths <math>x(t)</math>, starting from different initial points may cross, the solution may become multi-valued, at which point we have developed caustics.
We also have (even before showing that <math>u</math> is a solution)

:<math>\xi(x(t)) = \xi(x(0)) - \int_0^t \nabla_x H(x(s),\xi(x(s))) \, ds.</math>

It remains to show that <math>\xi</math>, which we have defined in a neighborhood of our initial plane, is the gradient of some function <math>u</math>.  This will follow if we show that the vector field <math>\xi</math> is curl free.  Consider the first term in the definition of <math>\xi</math>.  This term, <math>\xi(x(0)) = \nabla u(x(0))</math> is curl free as it is the gradient of a function.  As for the other term, we note

:<math>\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_k \, \partial x_j} H = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_j \, \partial x_k} H. </math>

The result follows.

==Applications==
{{prose|section|date=May 2025}}
{{unsourced section|date=May 2025}}
* A concrete application is the [[computation of radiowave attenuation in the atmosphere]].
* Finding the [[Shape from Shading|shape from shading]] in computer vision.
* Geometric optics
* Continuous shortest path problems
* Image segmentation
* Study of the shape for a solid propellant rocket grain

===Optics, oceanology and quantum mechanics===
The analogy between the three fields of optics, [[oceanology]]<ref>{{cite web
 |last=Feddersen
 |first=Falk
 |title=Waves in the Ocean: Linear Treatment
 |url=https://falk.ucsd.edu/pdf/LinearWaveNotes_4March2019.pdf
 |publisher=Scripps Institution of Oceanography, University of California San Diego
 |date=2019-03-04
 |access-date=2026-03-27
}}</ref> and quantum mechanics can be summarized in the following table. The first row shows the full wave equations from optics, oceanology and QM, namely the [[Helmholtz equation]], the PDE governing the sea surface elevation <math>\eta</math> and the [[Schrödinger equation|Schrödinger equation]] respectively.

The second row is the first order [[WKB approximation]], i.e. the slowly varying amplitude variation and the equations obtained are the Eikonal equation of optics and oceanology and the Hamilton-Jacobi equation. 

{| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center;"
! Scope !! Optics !! Oceanology !! Quantum mechanics
|-
! Full wave equation
| <math>\nabla^2 \psi - \frac{1}{c^2(x)} \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial t^2} = 0</math>
| <math>\frac{\partial ^2 \eta  }{\partial x^2} = g \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(h\frac{\partial \eta}{\partial x}\right)</math>
| <math>i\hbar \,\partial_t \psi = \hat{H}\psi</math>
|-
! Eikonal equation
| <math>|\nabla S(x)|^2 = n^2(x)</math>
| <math>\partial_t S + \omega(x,\nabla S) = 0</math>
| <math>\partial_t S + H(x,\nabla S,t) = 0</math>
|}
